topics.title: Primes, HCF and LCM
topics.intro: Every whole number above 1 is built from primes in exactly one way: its prime factorisation. Once you have it, HCFs and LCMs fall out almost for free.
topics.teach: Explain how prime factorisation helps you find the LCM of 84 and 90.
topics.talk: Ask {him} why 1 is not counted as a prime number.
topics.hook: Primes are the building blocks: **HCF** takes the primes both numbers share; **LCM** takes every prime, at its highest power.

visual.caption: Divide by primes until you reach 1: 84 = 2 × 2 × 3 × 7 = 2² × 3 × 7.
Primes of 84 and 90. The overlap gives the HCF: 2 × 3 = 6. Everything in the circles gives the LCM: 2 × 7 × 2 × 3 × 3 × 5 = 1260.

topics.title: Powers, roots and the order of operations
topics.intro: Powers are repeated multiplication, and the index laws (add, subtract, multiply the little numbers) follow from that. Negative and fractional indices are the same idea pushed further.
topics.teach: Explain why 5⁰ = 1 using the division law.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what 2⁻¹ means, and why.
topics.hook: **BIDMAS** sets the order; for powers, **multiply → add** the indices, **divide → subtract**, **power of a power → multiply**.

topics.title: Standard form
topics.intro: Astronomers and atom-scientists both need standard form: A × 10ⁿ with A at least 1 and less than 10. Big numbers have positive powers; tiny ones negative.
topics.teach: Explain how to multiply two numbers written in standard form.
topics.talk: The Sun is about 1.5 × 10⁸ km away. Ask {him} to write it out in full.
topics.hook: **A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10**: big numbers get a positive power, tiny ones a negative power.

head: metres
standard form
visual.caption: Rough sizes (the width of an atom and of a hair). A × 10ⁿ with 1 ≤ A < 10: big numbers have positive powers, tiny ones negative.

topics.title: Fractions: all four operations
topics.intro: Adding needs a common denominator; multiplying doesn’t; dividing means multiplying by the reciprocal. Mixed numbers become improper fractions first.
topics.teach: Explain why dividing by {{2/3}} is the same as multiplying by {{3/2}}.
topics.talk: Ask {him} how many {{3/4}}-hour lessons fit into 4½ hours.
topics.hook: Adding? Find a common denominator. Dividing? **Keep, Change, Flip**.

visual.caption: {{2/3}} = {{4/6}} = {{8/12}}: equivalent fractions line up on the fraction wall.

topics.title: Percentage change, reverse and compound
topics.intro: Multipliers make percentages quick: a 15% increase is × 1.15. Reverse percentages divide by the multiplier; compound interest multiplies again and again.
topics.teach: Explain why a 20% rise followed by a 20% fall leaves you worse off.
topics.talk: Find a sale price in a shop and ask {him} for the original price.
topics.hook: Percentages are multipliers: **+15% is × 1.15, −15% is × 0.85**. Reverse a change by dividing.

visual.caption: Each box is 20%. A 20% rise adds 1 box: × 1.2. Reverse: if the new price is £60, then 6 boxes = £60, so 1 box = £10 and the original was 5 boxes = £50.

topics.title: Ratio and proportion
topics.intro: Ratio compares parts; proportion scales them. Direct proportion goes up together, inverse proportion trades off: more workers, fewer days.
topics.teach: Explain how to tell whether a problem is direct or inverse proportion.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which pack of something in the cupboard is the better value per 100 g.
topics.hook: **Add the parts, share the total, multiply back**: find what one part is worth first.

visual.caption: Share 40 drachmae in the ratio 3 : 2. 5 equal parts = 40, so 1 part = 8: Kit gets 24 and Mira 16.

topics.title: Algebra: simplify, expand and factorise
topics.intro: Algebra is arithmetic with the numbers left unknown. Expanding multiplies out brackets; factorising puts them back. Each undoes the other.
topics.teach: Explain how you know you have factorised fully.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to factorise 12x + 18 and check by expanding.
topics.hook: Expanding and factorising are opposites, like zipping and unzipping a coat.

visual.caption: The grid (area) method: 3(2x + 5) = 6x + 15. Read it backwards to factorise: 6x + 15 = 3(2x + 5).

topics.title: Substitution and rearranging formulae
topics.intro: Physics, finance and engineering run on formulae. Substitute carefully (brackets round negatives!), and rearrange by undoing the operations in reverse order.
topics.teach: Explain how to make r the subject of A = πr².
topics.talk: Ask {him} to convert today’s temperature to Fahrenheit using F = {{9/5}}C + 32.
topics.hook: Socks on, then shoes; shoes off, then socks: **rearrange by undoing in reverse order**.

topics.title: Linear equations
topics.intro: An equation is a balance: do the same to both sides. With unknowns on both sides, gather the x terms first; with fractions, multiply them away.
topics.teach: Explain how to solve 5(x − 2) = 3(x + 4).
topics.talk: I think of a number, multiply by 4 and subtract 7. I get the same as doubling it and adding 9. Ask {him} for the number.
topics.hook: An equation is a balance: **whatever you do to one side, do to the other**.

visual.caption: Do the same to both sides. Check: 5 × 9 = 45 and 3 × 15 = 45.

topics.title: Inequalities
topics.intro: Inequalities are solved like equations, with one twist: multiplying or dividing by a negative number flips the sign.
topics.teach: Explain why −2x > 6 gives x < −3, not x > −3.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for all the integers that satisfy −2 < n ≤ 3.
topics.hook: Solve like an equation, but **multiply or divide by a negative and the sign flips**.

head: inequality
on a number line
visual.caption: Open: 2 is not included. Filled: it is. Multiply or divide by a negative and the sign flips: −2x > 6 gives x < −3.

topics.title: Sequences and the nth term
topics.intro: A linear sequence goes up by the same amount each time, so its nth term is dn + c. If the differences themselves go up steadily, it is quadratic.
topics.teach: Explain how to decide whether 100 is in the sequence 4, 11, 18, …
topics.talk: Ask {him} for the nth term of 5, 8, 11, 14, … and its 100th term.
topics.hook: Linear nth term = **difference × n + the zero term** (the term before the first).

visual.caption: Up by 3 each time, so compare with 3n: every term is 2 more. nth term = 3n + 2.

topics.title: Straight-line graphs
topics.intro: In y = mx + c, m is the gradient (steepness) and c is where the line crosses the y-axis. Parallel lines share a gradient; perpendicular gradients multiply to −1.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the equation of a line from its graph.
topics.talk: Ask {him} which is steeper: y = 3x − 1 or y = −4x + 2.
topics.hook: **y = mx + c**: m is the gradient (rise ÷ run), c is where the line cuts the y-axis.

visual.caption: y = 2x + 1 and y = 2x − 3 are parallel: both have gradient 2. y = −½x + 2 is perpendicular to them, because 2 × −½ = −1.

topics.title: Angles in polygons and parallel lines
topics.intro: Exterior angles of any polygon add to 360°; interior angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. Between parallel lines, F angles and Z angles are equal and C angles add to 180°.
topics.teach: Explain why the interior angles of a hexagon add up to 720°.
topics.talk: Count the sides of a 50p coin and ask {him} for its exterior angle.
topics.hook: **F angles are equal, Z angles are equal, C angles add to 180°**. Exterior angles of any polygon total 360°.

head: n
angle sum
exterior
visual.caption: Interior angles add to (n − 2) × 180°. Exterior angles add to 360°, so each exterior angle of a regular polygon is 360° ÷ n.

topics.title: Area: trapezia and circles
topics.intro: A trapezium’s area is the average of the parallel sides times the height. For circles, Archimedes showed that π links the radius to both the circumference and the area.
topics.teach: Explain why the area of a trapezium is ½(a + b)h.
topics.talk: Measure round a plate and across it: ask {him} to estimate π.
topics.hook: “**Cherry pie’s delicious; apple pies are too**”: C = πd and A = πr².

visual.caption: Area = ½(a + b)h = ½ × (4 + 10) × 5 = 35 cm².

topics.title: Volume and surface area of prisms
topics.intro: Every prism has volume = cross-section × length; a cylinder is a prism with a circle for its cross-section. Surface area means unfolding the solid into a net.
topics.teach: Explain how to find the surface area of a cylinder.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to estimate how many litres a bath holds by measuring it.
topics.hook: Prism volume = **cross-section × length**, like a loaf of bread: every slice is the same shape.

visual.caption: Any prism: volume = area of cross-section × length. A cylinder is a prism with a circle for its cross-section: V = πr²h.

topics.title: Transformations, bearings and scale
topics.intro: Reflections, rotations, translations and enlargements move shapes on a grid. Bearings measure direction clockwise from north; scales turn maps into real distances.
topics.teach: Explain what happens to the area of a shape enlarged by scale factor 3.
topics.talk: Use a map app together: ask {him} for the bearing from home to school.
topics.hook: Bearings: **from North, Clockwise, in Three figures** (045°, not 45°).

head: transformation
to describe it, give
rows: the mirror line, e.g. y = x
visual.caption: Bearings are measured clockwise from north, with three figures: east is 090°.

topics.title: Probability
topics.intro: Probabilities run from 0 to 1. Sample spaces list every outcome; Venn diagrams sort overlapping groups; for independent events, multiply.
topics.teach: Explain why the probability of “at least one” is 1 − P(none).
topics.talk: Roll two dice 36 times and compare how often you get a total of 7 with the theory.
topics.hook: All the outcomes add to 1, so **P(not A) = 1 − P(A)**. Independent events: **AND means multiply**.

visual.caption: Two dice: 36 equally likely outcomes. A total of 7 happens in 6 of them, so P(7) = {{6/36}} = {{1/6}}.

topics.title: Statistics: averages and grouped data
topics.intro: Mean, median and mode each answer “what is typical?” differently. From frequency tables, multiply before you add; for grouped data, midpoints give an estimate.
topics.teach: Explain when the median is a better average than the mean.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to find the mean and median of the family’s shoe sizes.
topics.hook: **Mo**de = **mo**st, **med**ian = **mid**dle, mean = add them up and share fairly.

head: goals
matches (f)
goals × f
visual.caption: Multiply before you add: mean = 29 ÷ 20 = 1.45 goals a match.

topics.title: Proof and mathematical reasoning
topics.intro: Mathematicians since Euclid have not been content with examples: they want proof. Algebra lets you prove something for EVERY number at once.
topics.teach: Prove that the sum of three consecutive integers is a multiple of 3.
topics.talk: Ask {him} for a counterexample to “all prime numbers are odd”.
topics.hook: A million examples never prove a rule, but **one counterexample destroys it**.

topics.title: The language of maths
topics.intro: Precise words matter: an expression is not an equation, a factor is not a multiple, and an identity is true for every value.
topics.teach: Explain the difference between an equation, an expression, a formula and an identity.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to give an example of each: expression, equation, formula.
topics.hook: **Sum** add, **difference** subtract, **product** multiply, **quotient** divide.

topics.title: Pythagoras’ theorem
topics.intro: In a right-angled triangle, a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse. Pythagoras’ followers in ancient Croton treated numbers almost as sacred.
topics.teach: Explain how to tell whether you add or subtract the squares.
topics.talk: Ask {him} whether a 6, 8, 10 triangle is right-angled, and why.
topics.hook: **a² + b² = c²**, where c, the hypotenuse, is always the longest side, opposite the right angle.

visual.caption: a² + b² = c², where c is the hypotenuse, opposite the right angle. 3² + 4² = 9 + 16 = 25 = 5².

topics.title: Simultaneous equations
topics.intro: Two equations, two unknowns: add or subtract the equations to eliminate one letter, solve for the other, then substitute back.
topics.teach: Explain why you might multiply one equation before eliminating.
topics.talk: Two lyres and an owl cost 17 drachmae; one lyre and an owl cost 11. Ask {him} the price of each.
topics.hook: **Same Signs Subtract**: if the terms you want to eliminate have the same sign, subtract; if not, add.

visual.caption: y = x + 1 and x + y = 7 cross at (3, 4): x = 3, y = 4 is the one pair that fits both equations.

topics.title: Quadratics: double brackets and factorising
topics.intro: Multiplying (x + a)(x + b) gives x² + (a + b)x + ab. Factorising runs this backwards: find two numbers that multiply to the constant and add to the middle number.
topics.teach: Explain how to factorise x² + 7x + 12.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to expand (x + 3)² and spot why it is not x² + 9.
topics.hook: For x² + bx + c, find two numbers that **multiply to c and add to b**.

visual.caption: (x + 3)(x + 4) = x² + 7x + 12: the two numbers add to the middle (3 + 4 = 7) and multiply to the end (3 × 4 = 12).

topics.title: Trigonometry: SOH CAH TOA
topics.intro: In a right-angled triangle the ratios of the sides depend only on the angle. Hipparchus of Nicaea built the first trigonometric tables over 2,000 years ago to track the stars.
topics.teach: Explain how to choose between sin, cos and tan.
topics.talk: Ask {him} what tan 45° must be, and why.
topics.hook: **SOH CAH TOA**: Sin = Opposite ÷ Hypotenuse, Cos = Adjacent ÷ Hypotenuse, Tan = Opposite ÷ Adjacent.

visual.caption: Name the sides from the angle θ: opposite it, next to it (adjacent), and the hypotenuse.

topics.title: Recurring decimals and fractions
topics.intro: Every fraction is a terminating or a recurring decimal, and every recurring decimal is a fraction. A neat algebra trick (10x − x) proves it.
topics.teach: Explain how to write 0.7̇ as a fraction.
topics.talk: Ask {him} to prove that 0.9̇ = 1.
topics.hook: One digit repeating? Put it over **9**. Two repeating digits? Over **99**: 0.272727… = 27/99.

items.hook: Prime factor tree: keep splitting until every branch ends in a prime, then circle the primes.
items.example: Two buses leave together, one every 12 minutes, one every 18: they next leave together after LCM(12, 18) = 36 minutes.

items.hook: **BIDMAS**: Brackets, Indices, Division and Multiplication, then Addition and Subtraction.
items.example: Bacteria that double every 20 minutes are 2⁹ = 512 times as many after 3 hours: that is 9 doublings.

items.hook: Count the places the digits jump: that is the power. Big numbers get a **+** power, tiny ones a **−** power.
items.example: A human hair is about 8 × 10⁻⁵ m wide, and the Moon is about 3.8 × 10⁸ m away.

items.hook: Dividing fractions: **Keep, Change, Flip**. Keep the first, change ÷ to ×, flip the second.
items.example: A recipe for 4 needs 3/4 of a cup of sugar. For 6 people, multiply by 6/4 = 3/2: 9/8 cups.

items.hook: **Multiplier magic**: 20% off is × 0.8; adding 20% VAT is × 1.2. To undo a change, divide.
items.example: A jacket costs £60 including 20% VAT. Before VAT it was 60 ÷ 1.2 = £50, not £48.

items.hook: **Unitary method**: find the value of one part, then multiply up.
items.example: Squash mixed 1 : 4 with water: a 1-litre jug holds 200 ml of squash and 800 ml of water.

items.hook: Expanding: **everything inside the bracket gets multiplied**. Factorising: take out the highest common factor.
items.example: 3 bags, each holding x apples and 2 pears, make 3(x + 2) = 3x + 6 pieces of fruit.

items.hook: **Undo in reverse order**: the last thing done to the letter is the first thing you undo.
items.example: A taxi costs £3 plus £2 a mile: C = 3 + 2m. A £15 fare means m = (15 − 3) ÷ 2 = 6 miles.

items.hook: Think of a see-saw: **do the same to both sides** to keep it level.
items.example: A phone plan is £10 a month plus £2 per GB. A £24 bill means 10 + 2g = 24, so g = 7 GB.

items.hook: The crocodile’s mouth eats the bigger number. Multiply or divide by a negative? **Flip the sign**.
items.example: A ride says you must be at least 120 cm tall: h ≥ 120. Exactly 120 cm is allowed, so it is ≥, not >.

items.hook: nth term = **(difference)n + (zero term)**: for 4, 7, 10, … that is 3n + 1.
items.example: A taxi charging £3 plus £2 a mile gives fares of £5, £7, £9, …: nth term 2n + 3.

items.hook: **y = mx + c**: m is the gradient (rise ÷ run); c is the y-intercept, where the line crosses the y-axis.
items.example: A gym charges £20 to join plus £15 a month: cost y = 15x + 20. The gradient is the monthly fee.

items.hook: Parallel lines: **F** (corresponding) equal, **Z** (alternate) equal, **C** (co-interior) add to 180°.
items.example: A 50p coin is based on a regular heptagon (with curved sides), and each exterior angle of a regular heptagon is 360° ÷ 7 ≈ 51.4°.

items.hook: Trapezium: **add the parallel sides, halve, times the height**. Circle: **πr²**.
items.example: A 12-inch pizza (radius 6 in) has area 36π ≈ 113 in², over twice the 8-inch pizza’s 16π ≈ 50 in².

items.hook: Volume of a prism = **cross-section × length**; a cylinder is just πr² × h.
items.example: A tin 7 cm across and 11 cm tall holds about π × 3.5² × 11 ≈ 423 cm³.

items.hook: Bearings: **North, Clockwise, Three figures**. Enlarge by scale factor k and areas grow by k².
items.example: On a 1 : 25 000 map, 4 cm stands for 100 000 cm = 1 km on the ground.

items.hook: **P(not A) = 1 − P(A)**. For independent events, AND means multiply.
items.example: With a 0.3 chance of rain each day (independently), two dry days in a row has probability 0.7 × 0.7 = 0.49.

items.hook: **Mo**de = **mo**st; median = middle; mean = total ÷ how many. From a frequency table: multiply, then add.
items.example: A shoe shop’s mean size might be 5.7, a size nobody wears; the mode tells it which size to stock most.

items.hook: Finding the long side? Square, **add**, square root. A short side? Square, **subtract**, square root.
items.example: A 4 m ladder with its foot 1 m from a wall reaches √(16 − 1) = √15 ≈ 3.87 m up the wall.

items.hook: **Same Signs Subtract**: same sign on the term to remove? Subtract the equations. Different signs? Add.
items.example: 2 coffees and a cake cost £8; 1 coffee and a cake cost £5.50. Subtract: a coffee is £2.50, so the cake is £3.

items.hook: **FOIL** for double brackets: First, Outer, Inner, Last.
items.example: Make an x m square garden 2 m longer and 2 m wider and its area is (x + 2)² = x² + 4x + 4, not x² + 4.

items.hook: **SOH CAH TOA**: Sin = Opp ÷ Hyp, Cos = Adj ÷ Hyp, Tan = Opp ÷ Adj. Label the sides first.
items.example: Stand 20 m from a tree and look up 35° to its top: it is about 20 × tan 35° ≈ 14 m above your eyes.

items.hook: One repeating digit? Over **9**. Two? Over **99**: 0.272727… = 27/99 = 3/11.
items.example: Split £10 three ways and a calculator shows 3.333…: each share is exactly £10/3, which pennies can’t pay.

items.prompt: Which is a proof that the sum of three consecutive integers is always a multiple of 3?

options.text: 1 + 2 + 3 = 6 and 4 + 5 + 6 = 15, both multiples of 3
options.feedback: Examples are evidence, not proof: they don’t cover every case.

options.text: Every third number is a multiple of 3
options.feedback: True, but it doesn’t show the SUM is a multiple of 3.

items.explain: Writing the integers as n, n + 1, n + 2 covers every case at once, and 3(n + 1) is clearly a multiple of 3.
items.hook: Three in a row? Call the middle one n: (n − 1) + n + (n + 1) = 3n.
items.example: Any three page numbers in a row, like 41, 42 and 43, add to 3 × 42 = 126.

items.prompt: Odd numbers can be written 2n + 1. What is (2a + 1)(2b + 1), and what does it prove?

options.text: 2(2ab + a + b) + 1, so odd × odd is always odd
4ab + 2a + 2b + 1 = 4(ab + a + b) + 1, so it is 1 more than a multiple of 4
options.feedback: Check the factorising: 4(ab + a + b) = 4ab + 4a + 4b, not 4ab + 2a + 2b.

options.text: 4ab + 1, so odd × odd is always odd
options.feedback: 2a × 2b = 4ab, and there are two more terms.

items.explain: Anything of the form 2(…) + 1 is odd, so the product of two odd numbers is always odd.
items.hook: **Odd × odd = odd**; one even factor makes any product even.
items.example: 5 rows of 7 chairs make 35 seats: odd × odd, so the seats can never all be paired up.

items.prompt: Which is a counterexample to “all prime numbers are odd”?

options.feedback: 9 is odd and not prime: it doesn’t contradict the claim.
1 is not a prime number.

items.explain: 2 is prime and even, so one example is enough to disprove the claim.
items.hook: **2 is the odd one out**: the only even prime.
items.example: Black swans, seen by European sailors in Australia in 1697, disproved “all swans are white”: a real counterexample.

items.prompt: Kit says −3² = 9. Theo says −3² = −9. Who is right?

options.text: Theo: only the 3 is squared, so −3² = −9
Kit: a negative number squared is always positive
options.feedback: That is true of (−3)², with brackets. Without brackets the minus waits until after the square.

options.text: Both, depending on the calculator
options.feedback: The convention is fixed: indices before the minus sign.

items.explain: Without brackets, indices come first: −3² = −9. With brackets, (−3)² = 9.
items.hook: **BIDMAS**: indices come before the minus sign. Want the negative squared? Use brackets: (−3)².
items.example: Type −3² into many calculators and you get −9; type (−3)² to get 9.

items.prompt: Is (a + b)² the same as a² + b²?

options.text: No: (a + b)² = a² + 2ab + b²
Yes, always
Only for negative numbers
options.feedback: It fails for almost every pair, e.g. 1 and 2.

items.explain: Expanding (a + b)(a + b) gives four terms: a² + ab + ab + b².
items.hook: (a + b)² means (a + b)(a + b): **four terms, two of them ab**. Don’t lose the middle!
items.example: Grow a 10 cm square tile by 2 cm each way: 12² = 144 = 100 + 40 + 4, not 100 + 4.

visual.caption: (a + b)² has four parts: a² + 2ab + b². The two ab pieces are what a² + b² leaves out.

items.prompt: A price goes up 10% and then down 10%. What happens overall?

options.text: It ends 1% lower than it started
It ends exactly where it started
options.feedback: The 10% fall is of a BIGGER amount: 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99.

options.text: It ends 1% higher than it started
options.feedback: 1.1 × 0.9 = 0.99, which is a decrease.

items.explain: Multipliers: 1.10 × 0.90 = 0.99, a 1% decrease overall.
items.hook: Up 10% then down 10% is × 1.1 × 0.9 = **× 0.99**: the fall is 10% of a bigger number.
items.example: A £100 game rises to £110, then a 10% sale cuts it to £99.

items.prompt: “Dividing always makes a number smaller.” Always, sometimes or never true?

options.text: Sometimes: dividing by 0.5 doubles a number
Always true: you are sharing it into parts
options.feedback: Try 6 ÷ ½ = 12.

options.text: Always true, except when you divide by 1
options.feedback: Try 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12: dividing by a number below 1 makes it bigger.

items.explain: Dividing by a number less than 1 (but more than 0) increases the answer: 6 ÷ 0.5 = 12.
items.hook: Dividing by a half means **how many halves fit in?** So it doubles.
items.example: Cut 6 pizzas into halves and you get 6 ÷ ½ = 12 pieces.

items.prompt: Eight athletes run a race in 12, 12, 13, 13, 14, 14, 15 and 41 seconds (one fell). Which average best describes a typical time?

options.text: The median (13.5 s)
The mean (16.75 s), because it uses every time
options.feedback: The 41-second fall drags the mean far above every other time.

options.text: The range (29 s)
options.feedback: The range measures spread, not a typical value.

items.explain: The median ignores how extreme the outlier is, so it represents the typical runner better.
items.hook: Outlier alert: one extreme value drags the **mean**, but the **median** stays in the middle.
items.example: If a billionaire walks into a café, the mean wealth soars, but the median customer is no richer.

items.prompt: A scatter graph shows that towns with more ice-cream sales have more sunburn cases. What can you conclude?

options.text: They are correlated, but that does not prove one causes the other
Ice cream causes sunburn, so sales should be limited
options.feedback: Correlation is not causation: a third factor (sunshine) explains both.

options.text: There is no relationship, because it is a coincidence
options.feedback: There is a relationship (a positive correlation), just not a causal one.

items.explain: Correlation shows the two move together; it does not prove that one causes the other.
items.hook: **Correlation is not causation**: look for a hidden third factor.
items.example: Sales of sun cream and of ice lollies rise together because both follow the sunshine.

items.prompt: The Pythagoreans discovered that √2 cannot be written as a fraction. What is such a number called?

options.text: irrational
recurring
options.feedback: Recurring decimals CAN be written as fractions.

options.text: prime
options.feedback: Primes are whole numbers with exactly two factors.

items.explain: Irrational numbers (√2, π) have decimals that never end and never repeat. Legend says the discovery shocked the Pythagoreans.
items.hook: Irrational = **can’t be written as a ratio**: its decimal never ends and never repeats.
items.example: An A4 sheet’s long side is √2 times its short side, so halving it keeps the same shape; √2 is irrational.

items.prompt: Eratosthenes measured the Earth around 240 BC. At noon the Sun was overhead at Syene but 7.2° from overhead at Alexandria, about 800 km north. Why does that give the Earth’s circumference?

options.text: 800 × 7.2 = 5,760 km, using the angle as a scale
options.feedback: The angle tells you what FRACTION of a full circle the distance is.
Compare 7.2° with the full 360°: it is one fiftieth.

items.explain: The distance between the cities is the same fraction of the circumference as 7.2° is of 360°: {{1/50}}. 50 × 800 km = 40,000 km, remarkably close to the true value.
items.hook: Angle fraction = distance fraction: **7.2° is 1/50 of 360°**.
items.example: Sailors once found their latitude the same way, by measuring the angle of the Sun at noon.

items.prompt: n² + n is always even, for any whole number n. Why?

options.text: n² + n = n(n + 1), and one of n, n + 1 is even
Because n² and n are always both even
options.feedback: n² is odd when n is odd: 3² = 9.

options.text: Because square numbers always end in 0, 4 or 6
options.feedback: Squares can end in 1, 5 or 9 too.

items.explain: Factorising gives n(n + 1): two consecutive whole numbers, one of which must be even, so the product is even.
items.hook: **Two neighbours, one is even**: so n(n + 1) is always even.
items.example: Take any two dates in a row, like the 14th and 15th: one is even, so their product is even.

items.prompt: What is 3x + 2 called (it has no equals sign)?
items.explain: An expression is a collection of terms with no equals sign.
items.hook: **No equals sign, no equation**: an expression is like a phrase without a verb.
items.example: The cost of x cinema tickets at £8 plus £2 for popcorn is the expression 8x + 2: no answer yet.

items.prompt: What is 3x + 2 = 11 called?
items.explain: An equation is true only for particular values (here x = 3).
items.hook: An equation is **a question with an answer**: only some values make it true.
items.example: I spent £34 on £8 tickets plus £2 popcorn: 8x + 2 = 34, so x = 4 tickets.

items.prompt: 2(x + 3) ≡ 2x + 6 is true for every value of x. What is it called?
items.explain: An identity (≡) is true whatever the value of the letter.
items.hook: Three bars, ≡, mean **always, always, always true**, whatever the value.
items.example: Doubling a bill of x + 3 pounds always gives 2x + 6 pounds, whatever x is: 2(x + 3) ≡ 2x + 6.

items.prompt: A = πr² connects different quantities. What is it called?
items.explain: A formula is a rule linking two or more quantities.
items.hook: A formula is **a recipe linking quantities**: put values in, get a value out.
items.example: Average speed cameras use speed = distance ÷ time: 1 km in 30 seconds means 120 km/h.

items.prompt: In 7x² − 3x, what is the number −3 called?
items.explain: A coefficient is the number multiplying a letter.
items.hook: The coefficient **co-operates** with the letter: it is the number stuck to its front, sign included.
items.example: In a phone bill of 5 + 2g pounds (£2 per GB), the coefficient 2 is the price of each gigabyte.

items.prompt: What is the reciprocal of {{4/7}}?
items.explain: The reciprocal is 1 divided by the number: flip the fraction. A number times its reciprocal is 1.
items.hook: **Flip it**: the reciprocal of a/b is b/a, and a number × its reciprocal = 1.
items.example: If 4 cups of rice make 7 portions, 1 portion needs 4/7 of a cup and 1 cup makes 7/4 portions.

items.prompt: Which word means a whole number that can be positive, negative or zero?
items.explain: …, −2, −1, 0, 1, 2, … are the integers.
items.hook: Integer is Latin for **whole, untouched**: no fractions, but positive, negative or zero.
items.example: Lift buttons are integers: −2, −1, 0 for the ground floor, then 1, 2, 3 …

items.prompt: A number that can be written as a fraction of two integers is called…
items.explain: Rational comes from “ratio”: 0.75 = 3/4 and 0.3̇ = 1/3 are rational; √2 and π are not.
items.hook: Rational contains **ratio**: if it can be a fraction of two integers, it is rational.
items.example: Every price in pounds and pence is rational: £2.49 = 249/100 of a pound.

items.prompt: What does “product” mean in maths?
items.explain: Sum: add. Difference: subtract. Product: multiply. Quotient: divide.
items.hook: **Sum** add, **difference** subtract, **product** multiply, **quotient** divide.
items.example: A café’s takings are the product of price and number sold: 30 drinks at £2 make £60.

items.prompt: What is the quotient of 36 and 4?
items.explain: The quotient is the result of division: 36 ÷ 4 = 9.
items.hook: Quotient comes from Latin **quot, “how many”**: how many times one number goes into another.
items.example: 36 sweets shared between 4 friends: the quotient is 9 each.

items.prompt: What is the longest side of a right-angled triangle called?
items.explain: From the Greek hypoteinousa, “stretching under” the right angle.
items.hook: The hypotenuse is **always opposite the right angle**, and always the longest side.
items.example: On a wheelchair ramp, the sloping surface is the hypotenuse; the ground and the rise are the other two sides.

visual.caption: The hypotenuse is the longest side, opposite the right angle.

items.prompt: What is a 10-sided polygon called? (deka is Greek for ten)
items.explain: Polygon names are Greek: pente (5) pentagon, hex (6) hexagon, okto (8) octagon, deka (10) decagon, dodeka (12) dodecagon.
items.hook: An **oct**opus has 8 arms and an **oct**agon 8 sides; a **dec**ade is 10 years and a **dec**agon 10 sides.
items.example: The UK 20p and 50p coins are based on heptagons: they have 7 sides, each slightly curved so the coin is the same width in every direction.

items.prompt: Isosceles comes from Greek isos (equal) + skelos (leg). What does an isosceles triangle have?
items.explain: Two equal “legs”, and so two equal base angles.
items.hook: **Isos = equal, skelos = leg**: two equal legs, and two equal base angles.
items.example: The end wall of a house under a pitched roof is usually an isosceles triangle on top of a rectangle.

items.prompt: Lines that meet at right angles are called…
items.explain: Perpendicular lines meet at 90°; parallel lines never meet.
items.hook: Perpendicular comes from **a plumb line**, a weight on a string that hangs at 90° to level ground.
items.example: The lines of a noughts-and-crosses grid and the corners of a door frame are perpendicular.
